turns.prompt_text: Have good 3d model outlines been created? Like a cartoon effect for video? I like the ones used in some youtube channels, but for video this would be nice, although I doubt it could be dine in real time without special heuristical methods and accepted lower quality.
turns.response_html:
You might be surprised by how solved this problem actually is. Real-time cartoon outlines—often called cel shading or toon shading—don't require you to sacrifice quality or rely on messy heuristics. In fact, they run flawlessly at 60+ frames per second in massive open-world games like Zelda: Breath of the Wild and Genshin Impact, as well as in real-time 3D animation pipelines.

The industry has largely settled on two extremely efficient real-time methods to achieve this look.

1. The "Inverted Hull" Trick (Mesh-Based)

This is the oldest, cheapest, and most common way to get perfectly crisp outlines in real time. It relies on a rendering quirk rather than complex math.

Here is how it works:

  1. Duplicate the 3D model.
  2. Inflate the duplicate slightly by pushing its vertices outward along their normals (making it slightly fatter than the original).
  3. Color the inflated duplicate entirely black.
  4. Flip the normals (the direction the polygons face) of the duplicate to point inward, and tell the rendering engine to enable "backface culling" (which hides the front of polygons).

The result? You render the original model normally, but behind it, you render the inside-out black shell. The black shell peaks out perfectly around the edges of your model, creating a flawless outline.

This method is practically free for a modern GPU to compute, making it the go-to for real-time video and game engines.

2. Screen Space Edge Detection (Post-Processing)

If duplicating geometry is too heavy (for example, in a scene with millions of polygons), engines use a post-processing shader. This method analyzes the entire frame as a 2D image after the 3D geometry is rendered, but before it reaches your screen.

The shader looks at two specific buffers (layers of data) generated by the camera:

  • The Depth Buffer: It looks for sudden jumps in distance. If pixel A is 5 feet away and the pixel next to it is 50 feet away, the shader draws a black line between them.
  • The Normal Buffer: It looks for sudden changes in the angle of the geometry. If a surface suddenly bends 90 degrees (like the corner of a cube), it draws a line.

This creates highly accurate outlines across the entire screen simultaneously, and it scales perfectly for 4K video rendering.

Both methods can easily be set up in real-time software like Unreal Engine, Unity, or Blender (using the EEVEE rendering engine) to record video without any quality drop or rendering wait times.

turns.prompt_text: Ok, but what about for video, this would require recreating a 3d scene from a series of images
turns.response_html:
Ah, I misunderstood—you're talking about applying this effect to existing 2D video (like live-action footage), not rendering a native 3D scene.

You have the exact right intuition: to use 3D outline methods on a flat video, the computer has to somehow figure out the 3D geometry from a series of 2D pixels. Doing a full frame-by-frame 3D reconstruction (like photogrammetry) would indeed be far too slow and messy for real-time video.

However, modern workflows tackle this without rebuilding the 3D mesh at all. They use one of three methods depending on the required quality.

1. AI Depth Estimation (The "Faked 3D" Route)

Instead of calculating a full 3D environment, modern tools use Monocular Depth Estimation. An AI model analyzes the flat video frame and instantly generates a grayscale "depth map" where white pixels are close to the camera and black pixels are far away.

Once you have this depth map, you apply the exact same "Screen Space Edge Detection" shader I mentioned earlier. The shader looks at the grayscale depth map, spots where the shades jump drastically (e.g., a person in the foreground against a background), and draws a clean black line there. Tools like Runway ML or After Effects (using depth passes) can process this surprisingly fast.

2. 2D Edge Detection (The Computer Vision Route)

If you want to bypass 3D entirely, you can process the video frames sequentially through an OpenCV pipeline. Using a Canny edge detector or a Sobel operator, the script analyzes the image for sharp contrast changes or color gradients instead of depth.

It finds those harsh pixel gradients and draws lines there. This is extremely computationally cheap and can easily run in real-time. The trade-off is that it's highly dependent on lighting. If a person wearing a black shirt stands in front of a black wall, a pure 2D edge detector won't "see" the edge of their shoulder, whereas a depth map would.

3. Temporal Style Transfer (The Modern Route)

This is how most high-end "cartoon filters" on video are done today. Using software like EbSynth or Stable Diffusion Video:

  1. You take a single frame of your video.
  2. You draw perfect cartoon outlines over it (or have an AI style it).
  3. The software analyzes the motion vectors of the pixels in the video (how things are moving from frame to frame) and "sticks" your drawn outlines to the moving pixels.

It doesn't understand the 3D space; it just understands that a cluster of pixels moved left, so it moves the outline left.

turns.prompt_text: Yes but I don't find them reliable enough, I believe it is because they don't make a 3d scene. I really think that would help out, by measuring standard items in the environment, the 3d scene could be relationally trilateralized
turns.response_html:
You are completely right about the reliability issue. The biggest flaw with 2D methods (like OpenCV edge detection or AI depth maps) on live-action video is "temporal flickering." Because the script evaluates every frame in isolation, a shadow shifting slightly can cause an outline to jump or disappear in the next frame. It doesn't have the spatial awareness that a true 3D scene provides.

Your idea of measuring standard items in the environment to anchor the math is a highly effective, proven concept. In computer vision, rather than trilateralization, this is done using triangulation through a process called Structure from Motion (SfM) or SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping).

Here is how a pipeline like that actually works.

1. Feature Tracking and Triangulation

Instead of looking at a single frame, the software tracks high-contrast pixels (features) as they move across multiple frames. Because the camera is moving, objects closer to the lens shift faster than objects in the background (parallax).

By calculating the angles between these points across different frames, the algorithm triangulates the exact 3D position of both the camera and the points in space, creating a 3D "point cloud."

2. Setting the Scale (The "Standard Item" Method)

This is where your idea comes in. A raw point cloud generated from video is essentially dimensionless—the computer knows the proportions of the scene, but it doesn't know if the room is 10 feet wide or 10 miles wide.

You're describing a core principle of spatial calibration. By identifying an object with a known real-world dimension in the footage—much like placing a reference coin in a 2D photo to calibrate parametric scale before running it through an OpenCV vector trace—you can force the software to lock the entire 3D point cloud to a physical ground truth. Once anchored, the geometry becomes highly reliable.

The Catch: Non-Rigid Bodies

This approach is currently used in high-end VFX (like match-moving in Hollywood) and drone mapping. It works flawlessly for generating perfect 3D environments and static objects.

The reason it isn't the standard for applying cartoon filters to people in real-time video is because of non-rigid body dynamics.

Structure from Motion relies on the assumption that the environment is static and only the camera is moving. If you film a person walking, their arms and legs are moving independently of the camera. The triangulation math breaks down because the "points" on their arm are shifting in ways that defy the camera's movement. Reconstructing a dense, moving, deforming 3D mesh (like a person's face talking) purely from a single 2D video lens is incredibly computationally heavy and prone to artifacting.

However, emerging tech like Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) and 4D Gaussian Splatting are getting remarkably close to solving this. They use AI to reconstruct moving 3D scenes from 2D video, providing that temporal stability you're looking for without needing manual frame-by-frame tracing.

turns.prompt_text: Interesting, perhaps a layering approach may help, stable items and walls are recorded, while active items are dropped
turns.response_html:
You've just described exactly how high-end visual effects pipelines solve this problem. Splitting the rigid, predictable background from the unpredictable, dynamic foreground is the standard way to prevent the math from breaking down.

In computer vision and VFX, this layering approach is achieved through Semantic Segmentation and Outlier Rejection.

Since you already have experience building Python image processing pipelines with OpenCV, prototyping a layered approach like this is surprisingly straightforward.

The Layered Pipeline

Instead of trying to calculate the 3D geometry of the entire video at once, the system splits the processing into two distinct streams using node-based logic.

Layer 1: The Rigid Background (SLAM)

The first step is to tell the tracking algorithm (like Structure from Motion) to completely ignore anything that moves independently.

  • Outlier Rejection: As the algorithm tracks high-contrast points across frames, it mathematically flags points that don't conform to the camera's general motion vector.
  • If the camera pans left, all the points on the walls shift right at a predictable mathematical rate. If a person is walking through the frame, the points on their swinging arms move at the "wrong" rate. The algorithm drops those points from the 3D calculation entirely.
  • The result is a highly stable, trilateralized 3D point cloud of just the empty room and stable objects.

Layer 2: The Active Foreground (Segmentation)

To handle the active items (the people) that were dropped from the 3D solve, the pipeline switches back to 2D image processing.

  • An AI model (like Mask R-CNN) or a background subtraction script analyzes the 2D video frames.
  • It creates a black-and-white matte (a mask) that perfectly silhouettes the moving subjects, essentially cutting them out of the video.
  • You can then apply standard 2D edge detection (like a Canny filter) or a localized depth-map pass only to these isolated, active elements. Because the background is gone, the edge detector doesn't get confused by shadows on the wall behind the person.

The Recombination

Finally, the two layers are composited back together. You render your rock-solid 3D background with perfect cartoon outlines, and then you overlay your masked, 2D-processed active subjects on top.

Because the stable items were calculated in true 3D space, the camera movements will feel perfectly grounded, and any minor flickering on the active foreground elements will be far less noticeable against the rock-solid background.
